screens.title: What is Prop Dressing?
screens.narratorSegment: Prop dressing refers to the deliberate placement of 3D assets within a scene to suggest history, use, and inhabitation. It's more than decoration: each object should imply why it is there and how it relates to characters or functions in the world. For instance, a market corner might include stacked crates, an overturned barrel, a leaning broom, and footprints — these details imply daily activity without any text. A common misconception is that more props always equal better storytelling. In reality, indiscriminate prop dumping dilutes narrative focus and taxes performance. Instead, choose props with purpose and compose them into clusters that read well at player viewpoints. A useful practice is to ask: who used this space, and what did they do here? Place props to answer that question — a cluster of crates near a stall suggests trade, tools by a door suggest recent maintenance. Key takeaway: prop dressing combines artistic intent with technical placement; it requires both the right objects and a disciplined approach to arrangement that supports the scene's story. What is Prop Dressing? means intentional placement of props to convey narrative, not just to fill space.. In practical terms, arranging props to tell a story and support immersion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › What is Prop Dressing?
Definition & Purpose
Prop dressing arranges objects to imply history, activity, and ownership. Each prop should serve the scene's narrative and composition.
Metaphor: Think of props as short sentences that together tell the room's story.
Misconception: Avoid 'more is better' — intentional choice beats random clutter.
Why it matters: Proper dressing increases immersion and directs player attention.
Concrete example
Medieval market corner: stacked crates, spilled grain sacks, a knocked-over barrel, and a broom by a stall suggest recent activity and commerce.
Example Card
Clustered crates create believable focal points. Group 3–5 items with varied scale and rotation, then duplicate the cluster rather than single items.
Key Takeaway
Every prop should answer 'why is this here?'. Use clusters and small variations to imply use without overwhelming performance.

screens.title: Snapping Tools Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Snapping tools let you place objects precisely and consistently, cutting down alignment errors and iteration time. Vertex snapping binds an object's pivot to another object's vertex, which is essential when assembling modular architecture so edges meet exactly. Grid snapping forces object transforms to discrete increments, ensuring tiles and repeated architectural elements share consistent spacing. Surface snapping is an approximation technique — you can drop an object onto a collider surface or use custom scripts to project an asset onto terrain; this is useful when you want props to conform to sloped or uneven ground. A common misconception is to rely only on snapping and ignore visual checking. Snapping helps accuracy, but you still need to view the scene from multiple camera distances to confirm natural contact and overlap. Example: align a wall corner with vertex snapping, lay floor tiles with grid snapping, then place barrels using surface checks so they sit flush on slightly uneven ground. The practical flow: choose the snapping mode, position or duplicate, then visually verify and nudge slight offsets for realism. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Snapping Tools
Quick Reference: Snapping Modes
Vertex Snapping (V key)
Snap an object's pivot to a target vertex for exact joins. Use for modular architecture and stacked objects.
Grid Snapping
Set move snap values in Snap Settings to lock movement to a grid for uniform spacing.
Surface Snapping
Drop objects onto colliders or use custom surface projection to conform props to uneven terrain.
Practical checklist
  • 1. Choose snapping mode appropriate to the task.
  • 2. Align a base piece first, then place supporting props.
  • 3. Duplicate with offsets, then visually inspect from camera angles.
  • 4. Use small manual nudges to avoid perfectly even spacing for organic feel.
Example
Build a corner by vertex-snapping two wall sections, grid-snap the floor tiles, and then place barrels using surface checks so they conform to small height offsets.
Common Mistake
Relying only on one snapping mode can create hidden overlaps or gaps. Always verify visually.

screens.title: Vertex Snapping Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: Vertex snapping is a targeted, high-precision technique that snaps an object's pivot to a vertex on another mesh. It's indispensable for snapping modular architecture so seams align and edges sit flush. To use it, select an object, hold the key that activates vertex snapping, then drag the pivot to a target vertex until it 'locks'. An important practice is to set the pivot of modular pieces thoughtfully during modeling so their logical snap points match in Unity. A common misunderstanding is expecting vertex snapping to fix scale or rotation discrepancies. It only aligns positions; if your pieces differ in scale or orientation, you must correct those before snapping. A practical example: aligning a wooden beam inside a doorway — vertex-snap the beam's pivot to the doorway vertex to ensure the beam sits exactly against the frame. After snapping, examine the joint at multiple camera distances and angles to catch small gaps or interpenetrations. If you encounter mismatch, check pivot placement and mesh origin in the modeling package or adjust the object transform before snapping. Vertex Snapping Deep Dive means vertex snapping aligns pivots to vertices precisely, but pivot setup and consistent scale matter for correct results.. In practical terms, precision alignment for modular assemblies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Vertex Snapping
How Vertex Snapping Works
Snap a selected object's pivot to a vertex on another object for perfect contact points when assembling modular parts.
Practical steps
  1. Set clean pivots in your modeling package or use Unity's pivot tools.
  2. Select the object, hold the vertex snap key, drag to target vertex.
  3. Verify rotation and scale before snapping to avoid mismatch.
Pro tip: make small test snaps and then cancel to see how the pivot aligns before committing.
Example scenario
You have a modular wall and a window trim. Vertex-snap the trim pivot to a window corner vertex so the trim sits flush without manual numeric adjustment.
Common Mistake
Snapping without checking pivot placement leads to off-center or rotated joints. Fix the pivot first.
Key Takeaway
Vertex snapping is precise but depends on correct pivot and consistent scale — treat it as a precision tool, not an automatic fix for poorly authored assets.

screens.title: Grid and Surface Snapping
screens.narratorSegment: Grid and surface snapping address different needs. Grid snapping enforces uniform spacing by snapping transforms to fixed increments. Use it for floor tiles, fences, or aligned rows of architecture where consistent spacing matters. Surface snapping is about natural contact: if terrain or props are slightly uneven, you either use physics-based drops, place colliders to rest on, or use a surface-projection tool so props sit flush on slopes. A useful workflow is to combine them: grid-snap the primary architecture for structure, then surface-snap smaller props to conform to topography. A common misconception is that grid snapping creates organic layouts — it doesn't. Rely on grid snapping for structure, then introduce intentional offsets to avoid a mechanical look. Example: grid-snap floor tiles, then place plant groups with surface checks and slight random offsets so they nestle into crevices and look natural rather than floating or perfectly aligned. Grid and Surface Snapping means grid snapping for ordered structure; surface methods for natural contact and terrain conformity.. In practical terms, consistency and natural contact on uneven geometry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Practical
When building floors and walls, grid snapping prevents small spacing errors that compound across repeated pieces.

screens.title: Efficient Duplication Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Duplication is a daily task when dressing scenes, and small workflow choices change how natural repeated props feel. The basic duplicate shortcut duplicates a selection so you can move the copy immediately. For controlled repetition, use the same object as a Prefab and duplicate instances via project or hierarchy for consistent components. A useful pattern is 'cluster duplication' — create a small, varied group of 3–5 props, make that group a Prefab, then duplicate and scatter the group across the scene. This preserves believable clusters while keeping editing efficient. Remember to vary scale slightly, and rotate on the Y-axis randomly to break uniformity. A common mistake is duplicating many identical single props which creates visible tiling. Instead, duplicate groups and apply small offsets, then verify from the primary camera view. Example steps: duplicate a barrel, apply scale 0.95–1.05, randomize Y-rotation, then nudge position so barrels look settled rather than snapped exactly to a grid. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Duplication Patterns
Shortcuts & Workflows
Use Cmd/Ctrl + D for quick copies, and Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + D for controlled duplicates placed at the same position for offsetting.
Cluster Duplication
Group 3–5 varied props, make the group a Prefab, then duplicate that prefab to produce believable clusters without repetitive artifacts.
Pro tip: when duplicating many items, vary scale within a small range (0.9–1.1) and rotate on Y to break symmetry.
Example workflow
Create a crate cluster, save as Prefab. Duplicate the cluster, scatter with small offsets, then adjust one instance if needed for a unique detail.
Key Takeaway
Cluster-based duplication preserves variation while minimizing authoring time and maintaining editability via Prefabs.
Watchout
Excessive unique models are expensive; cluster duplication provides a middle ground between repetition and full uniqueness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PropRandomizer Script
Editor script (place in an Editor folder)
This script randomizes local scale and Y rotation for the currently selected GameObjects in the Editor.
// This is an Editor script, place it in an 'Editor' folder in your project.
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEditor;

public class PropRandomizer : EditorWindow
{
  float minScale = 0.9f;
  float maxScale = 1.1f;
  float rotationRange = 360f; // Max Y rotation in degrees

  [MenuItem("Tools/Prop Randomizer")]
  public static void ShowWindow()
  {
    GetWindow("Prop Randomizer");
  }

  void OnGUI()
  {
    GUILayout.Label("Randomize Selected Props", EditorStyles.boldLabel);

    minScale = EditorGUILayout.FloatField("Min Scale", minScale);
    maxScale = EditorGUILayout.FloatField("Max Scale", maxScale);
    rotationRange = EditorGUILayout.FloatField("Max Y Rotation", rotationRange);

    if (GUILayout.Button("Apply Randomization"))
    {
      RandomizeSelectedProps();
    }
  }

  void RandomizeSelectedProps()
  {
    foreach (GameObject obj in Selection.gameObjects)
    {
      // Randomize Scale
      float randomScale = Random.Range(minScale, maxScale);
      obj.transform.localScale = new Vector3(randomScale, randomScale, randomScale);

      // Randomize Y Rotation
      float randomRotationY = Random.Range(0f, rotationRange);
      obj.transform.localRotation = Quaternion.Euler(obj.transform.localRotation.eulerAngles.x, randomRotationY, obj.transform.localRotation.eulerAngles.z);

      // Mark scene as dirty to save changes
      EditorUtility.SetDirty(obj);
    }
    Debug.Log("Randomization applied to " + Selection.gameObjects.Length + " objects.");
  }
}
Explanation
  • Place script in an Editor folder so it compiles into the Editor assembly.
  • It exposes an EditorWindow UI for min/max scale and rotation range.
  • Selection.gameObjects is iterated and each transform is modified and marked dirty.
Use case
Run on a selection of crates to quickly create believable scale and rotation differences, then manually adjust outliers.

screens.title: Prefab Workflow and Instance Overrides
screens.narratorSegment: Prefabs are reusable GameObject assets that allow you to create a single source of truth for props and then instance them across scenes. The standard workflow: create a configured GameObject in the Hierarchy, drag it into the Project window to make a Prefab asset, then use instances of that Prefab in scenes. When you change the Prefab asset, every instance updates automatically — this is the powerful global editing behavior. You can also override properties per-instance, which is useful when you need a slight variation for a specific placement. A common mistake is editing the wrong layer — changing an instance without realizing it's an override leads to inconsistent results. Instead, open the Prefab asset or use 'Open Prefab' in the Inspector to make global edits. Example: build a barrel with collider, material and script, make it a Prefab, then scatter its instances. Later, to change the barrel's color everywhere, edit the Prefab asset once instead of editing each instance. Prefabs keep scenes consistent and let you scale dressing workflows across large environments. Prefab Workflow and Instance Overrides means use prefabs to maintain consistent props across scenes; edit the asset for global updates, and use overrides sparingly for local variation.. In practical terms, create, edit, and manage reusable prop assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Variety vs Repetition
screens.narratorSegment: Balancing variety and repetition is a central compositional challenge. Pure repetition — many identical props arranged in a grid — reads as artificial. Pure uniqueness — every asset different — can be costly and visually noisy. The effective strategy is intelligent repetition with variation. Use a small core set of Prefabs and vary scale, Y-rotation, and material instances slightly to create visual richness at low authoring cost. Grouping is also powerful: instead of scattering single rocks, create a rock cluster with three different rock models, vary their transforms, make that cluster a Prefab, then scatter cluster instances. Misconceptions include thinking rotation alone is enough; scale and material variation are equally important. Example: instead of 20 identical trees, use two or three trunk models, vary scale by 0.9–1.1, rotate Y randomly, and group a few to form copse variations. This yields believable forests with fewer unique models and better performance. In practical terms, find the balance between performance and visual interest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Pure Repetition
Many identical models, often in a grid. Fast to author but looks artificial and repetitive.
Controlled Variation

screens.title: Tiling Artifacts & Unnatural Distribution
screens.narratorSegment: Two frequent issues that break immersion are tiling artifacts and unnatural distribution. Tiling artifacts occur when a texture repeats over a large surface without interruption, revealing seams and pattern repetition. Fixes include adding decals or unique props to break up large surfaces, using material variations, or placing small props like crates and debris to distract the eye from uniform tiling. Unnatural distribution shows up as perfectly spaced props, straight lines, or floating objects. The cure is intentional randomness: vary position slightly, rotate on Y, and adjust scale. Also ensure props are grounded — objects floating even slightly above the surface are immediately noticeable. A common misconception is that small errors aren't seen; in practice camera movement and different viewing distances reveal these problems quickly. Example fixes: place a few scattered sacks and a barrel to break a tiled wall pattern, and nudge object positions by small amounts to create organic clusters rather than perfect rows. Tiling Artifacts & Unnatural Distribution means break tiles with decals or props, avoid exact spacing, and ensure objects sit firmly on the ground.. In practical terms, diagnose repetitive textures and mechanical placement, then fix them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Pitfalls & Fixes
Tiling Artifacts
Repeating textures show seams and patterns at scale. Break them with decals, unique props, or varied material instances.
Fix list
  • Place unique props along large surfaces.
  • Use decals or vertex paint to vary appearance.
  • Mix material instances with subtle parameter differences.
Unnatural Distribution
Even spacing and exact alignment look artificial. Use small offsets, grouping, and varied scales to produce organic patterns.
Common Mistake
Placing many copies without storytelling leads to an 'asset dump' — props need purpose and placement intent.
Example Fix
Scatter a few crates and a barrel near a wall seam to distract from tiling, and rotate/scale them slightly so they don't repeat visually.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn to convert bare modular geometry into believable, story-rich corners using efficient placement tools and artistic principles. Prop dressing is not about filling space; it's about showing history and action through objects. You will learn practical Unity techniques — like vertex and grid snapping — that make precise placement fast, and Prefab workflows that let you change hundreds of props from one asset. We'll also cover the compositional balance of variety and repetition so your scenes read as natural, not artificially tiled, and how to spot and fix common mistakes like floating props or texture tiling. A concrete example we'll revisit is a small medieval market corner: walls aligned with vertex snapping, crates grouped into informal clusters, and a barrel Prefab duplicated with slight scale and rotation variations to break up repetition. By the end you'll understand both the tools and the creative choices that make a scene feel used and believable. Think about the last environment you entered in a game — what story did the props tell? That perspective will guide every placement decision here.

These objectives focus on both technique and judgement. First, you'll master efficient placement tools so you can align and duplicate assets quickly and without error. That includes vertex snapping for exact joins and grid snapping for consistent spacing. Second, you'll use prop dressing as a storytelling tool, placing items to imply past actions and inhabitant behavior. This matters because props communicate narrative without words. Third, you'll apply composition rules — balancing repetition and controlled variation — to create believable clusters and avoid the artificial look of perfect grids. Finally, you'll adopt Prefabs for scalable asset management so changes propagate reliably across instances. A concrete example: after this chapter you should be able to build a small market corner by snapping modular walls, creating a crate Prefab, duplicating it while varying scale and rotation, and grouping clusters for natural distribution. We'll also verify competency milestones such as creating Prefabs, snapping modular pieces, and identifying and resolving tiling or floating prop issues. These skills save time and result in scenes that feel intentional.

We'll map these objectives to practical skills. 'Learn' covers basic tooling: you should be comfortable with vertex snapping and duplication shortcuts. 'Understand' means recognizing how prop choice and placement affect narrative and immersion. 'Apply' asks you to create Prefabs and duplicate them with intentional variation to populate a scene. 'Master' means managing asset sets across scenes and diagnosing issues like tiling artifacts or unnatural distribution. A useful example is building a market stall: at the learn stage you align boards with grid snapping; at understand you choose props that suggest trade; at apply you create a barrel Prefab and scatter duplicates with rotated Y values; at master you update a Prefab material and observe all instances change. We'll use these layers to structure practice: tool demos, guided dressing, Prefab workflows, and diagnosis checks. This ensures that skill gains transfer directly into faster iteration and more convincing environments.

Prop dressing refers to the deliberate placement of 3D assets within a scene to suggest history, use, and inhabitation. It's more than decoration: each object should imply why it is there and how it relates to characters or functions in the world. For instance, a market corner might include stacked crates, an overturned barrel, a leaning broom, and footprints — these details imply daily activity without any text. A common misconception is that more props always equal better storytelling. In reality, indiscriminate prop dumping dilutes narrative focus and taxes performance. Instead, choose props with purpose and compose them into clusters that read well at player viewpoints. A useful practice is to ask: who used this space, and what did they do here? Place props to answer that question — a cluster of crates near a stall suggests trade, tools by a door suggest recent maintenance. Key takeaway: prop dressing combines artistic intent with technical placement; it requires both the right objects and a disciplined approach to arrangement that supports the scene's story. What is Prop Dressing? means intentional placement of props to convey narrative, not just to fill space.. In practical terms, arranging props to tell a story and support immersion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Snapping tools let you place objects precisely and consistently, cutting down alignment errors and iteration time. Vertex snapping binds an object's pivot to another object's vertex, which is essential when assembling modular architecture so edges meet exactly. Grid snapping forces object transforms to discrete increments, ensuring tiles and repeated architectural elements share consistent spacing. Surface snapping is an approximation technique — you can drop an object onto a collider surface or use custom scripts to project an asset onto terrain; this is useful when you want props to conform to sloped or uneven ground. A common misconception is to rely only on snapping and ignore visual checking. Snapping helps accuracy, but you still need to view the scene from multiple camera distances to confirm natural contact and overlap. Example: align a wall corner with vertex snapping, lay floor tiles with grid snapping, then place barrels using surface checks so they sit flush on slightly uneven ground. The practical flow: choose the snapping mode, position or duplicate, then visually verify and nudge slight offsets for realism. Snapping Tools Overview means vertex snapping for precision, grid snapping for consistent spacing, and surface methods for natural contact.. In practical terms, speed and precision with vertex, grid, and surface techniques. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Vertex snapping is a targeted, high-precision technique that snaps an object's pivot to a vertex on another mesh. It's indispensable for snapping modular architecture so seams align and edges sit flush. To use it, select an object, hold the key that activates vertex snapping, then drag the pivot to a target vertex until it 'locks'. An important practice is to set the pivot of modular pieces thoughtfully during modeling so their logical snap points match in Unity. A common misunderstanding is expecting vertex snapping to fix scale or rotation discrepancies. It only aligns positions; if your pieces differ in scale or orientation, you must correct those before snapping. A practical example: aligning a wooden beam inside a doorway — vertex-snap the beam's pivot to the doorway vertex to ensure the beam sits exactly against the frame. After snapping, examine the joint at multiple camera distances and angles to catch small gaps or interpenetrations. If you encounter mismatch, check pivot placement and mesh origin in the modeling package or adjust the object transform before snapping. Vertex Snapping Deep Dive means vertex snapping aligns pivots to vertices precisely, but pivot setup and consistent scale matter for correct results.. In practical terms, precision alignment for modular assemblies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Grid and surface snapping address different needs. Grid snapping enforces uniform spacing by snapping transforms to fixed increments. Use it for floor tiles, fences, or aligned rows of architecture where consistent spacing matters. Surface snapping is about natural contact: if terrain or props are slightly uneven, you either use physics-based drops, place colliders to rest on, or use a surface-projection tool so props sit flush on slopes. A useful workflow is to combine them: grid-snap the primary architecture for structure, then surface-snap smaller props to conform to topography. A common misconception is that grid snapping creates organic layouts — it doesn't. Rely on grid snapping for structure, then introduce intentional offsets to avoid a mechanical look. Example: grid-snap floor tiles, then place plant groups with surface checks and slight random offsets so they nestle into crevices and look natural rather than floating or perfectly aligned. Grid and Surface Snapping means grid snapping for ordered structure; surface methods for natural contact and terrain conformity.. In practical terms, consistency and natural contact on uneven geometry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Duplication is a daily task when dressing scenes, and small workflow choices change how natural repeated props feel. The basic duplicate shortcut duplicates a selection so you can move the copy immediately. For controlled repetition, use the same object as a Prefab and duplicate instances via project or hierarchy for consistent components. A useful pattern is 'cluster duplication' — create a small, varied group of 3–5 props, make that group a Prefab, then duplicate and scatter the group across the scene. This preserves believable clusters while keeping editing efficient. Remember to vary scale slightly, and rotate on the Y-axis randomly to break uniformity. A common mistake is duplicating many identical single props which creates visible tiling. Instead, duplicate groups and apply small offsets, then verify from the primary camera view. Example steps: duplicate a barrel, apply scale 0.95–1.05, randomize Y-rotation, then nudge position so barrels look settled rather than snapped exactly to a grid. Efficient Duplication Patterns means duplicate varied groups, not identical singles. use prefabs plus subtle scale and rotation changes to avoid tiled repetition.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For many artists, a small editor utility reduces repetitive manual work. The PropRandomizer script in this chapter is an EditorWindow that randomizes scale and Y-axis rotation for selected GameObjects. This script is an optional productivity aid: it automates variation while letting you keep artistic control. In practice you set a min and max scale, a rotation range, and press Apply. A misconception is to treat such tools as replacements for composition judgment. They speed variation but you must still inspect and nudge results so props sit naturally. The code block below is an editor-only script that should live in an Editor folder. It iterates Selection. gameObjects, randomizes scale within chosen bounds, randomizes Y rotation, and marks objects dirty so changes persist. Use it as a starting point and extend it to add per-axis control, surface checks, or seed-based randomness. Try the tool on a set of crates to quickly produce believable size and orientation differences and then manually adjust outliers for best results. PropRandomizer Editor Script means editor scripts can automate repetitive variation, but always validate results for composition and contact with the environment.. In practical terms, a simple editor tool to randomize scale and y-rotation of selected props. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Prefabs are reusable GameObject assets that allow you to create a single source of truth for props and then instance them across scenes. The standard workflow: create a configured GameObject in the Hierarchy, drag it into the Project window to make a Prefab asset, then use instances of that Prefab in scenes. When you change the Prefab asset, every instance updates automatically — this is the powerful global editing behavior. You can also override properties per-instance, which is useful when you need a slight variation for a specific placement. A common mistake is editing the wrong layer — changing an instance without realizing it's an override leads to inconsistent results. Instead, open the Prefab asset or use 'Open Prefab' in the Inspector to make global edits. Example: build a barrel with collider, material and script, make it a Prefab, then scatter its instances. Later, to change the barrel's color everywhere, edit the Prefab asset once instead of editing each instance. Prefabs keep scenes consistent and let you scale dressing workflows across large environments. Balancing variety and repetition is a central compositional challenge. Pure repetition — many identical props arranged in a grid — reads as artificial. Pure uniqueness — every asset different — can be costly and visually noisy. The effective strategy is intelligent repetition with variation. Use a small core set of Prefabs and vary scale, Y-rotation, and material instances slightly to create visual richness at low authoring cost. Grouping is also powerful: instead of scattering single rocks, create a rock cluster with three different rock models, vary their transforms, make that cluster a Prefab, then scatter cluster instances. Misconceptions include thinking rotation alone is enough; scale and material variation are equally important. Example: instead of 20 identical trees, use two or three trunk models, vary scale by 0.9–1.1, rotate Y randomly, and group a few to form copse variations. This yields believable forests with fewer unique models and better performance. Variety vs Repetition means use a small set of assets with scale, rotation, and material tweaks, and duplicate clusters for believable variation with low cost.. Two frequent issues that break immersion are tiling artifacts and unnatural distribution. Tiling artifacts occur when a texture repeats over a large surface without interruption, revealing seams and pattern repetition. Fixes include adding decals or unique props to break up large surfaces, using material variations, or placing small props like crates and debris to distract the eye from uniform tiling. Unnatural distribution shows up as perfectly spaced props, straight lines, or floating objects. The cure is intentional randomness: vary position slightly, rotate on Y, and adjust scale. Also ensure props are grounded — objects floating even slightly above the surface are immediately noticeable. A common misconception is that small errors aren't seen; in practice camera movement and different viewing distances reveal these problems quickly. Example fixes: place a few scattered sacks and a barrel to break a tiled wall pattern, and nudge object positions by small amounts to create organic clusters rather than perfect rows. Tiling Artifacts & Unnatural Distribution means break tiles with decals or props, avoid exact spacing, and ensure objects sit firmly on the ground..
